lead: A cycloconverter turns AC of one frequency into AC of another frequency directly, with no DC link. It is two phase-controlled converters back to back, one for each direction of output current, building each output half cycle from pieces of the supply wave. Step-down works with natural commutation; step-up needs forced commutation. Large low-speed drives such as cement kilns, ore mills and ship propulsion use it.
prereq: You need: the single-phase and three-phase controlled rectifiers with their output formula (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α, and dual converters, from controlled and uncontrolled rectifiers.

blocks.text: The positive (P) group carries the load current one way and gives the positive output half cycles; the negative (N) group carries it the other way. In non-circulating mode only one group is fired at a time.

items: Single-phase to single-phase, midpoint: a centre-tapped transformer and four SCRs, two per group.
Single-phase to single-phase, bridge: two single-phase bridges in antiparallel, eight SCRs. Each group gives an average of (2Vm/π) cos α per half cycle, where Vm is the peak supply voltage.
Three-phase to single-phase: two three-phase bridges, twelve SCRs, each group giving (3VmL/π) cos α, with VmL the peak line voltage.
Three-phase to three-phase: three such converters, one per output phase: 18 SCRs with three-pulse groups or 36 with six-pulse bridges.

blocks.text: Step-down means f<sub>o</sub> < f<sub>s</sub>, where f<sub>o</sub> is the output and f<sub>s</sub> the supply frequency. In the simplest case f<sub>o</sub> = f<sub>s</sub>/3: the P group is fired at the same α in three supply half cycles, giving three positive humps, then the N group gives three negative humps. One output cycle spans three supply cycles. With a resistive load each hump is a phase-controlled half sine, so the RMS output is the AC-controller value V<sub>s</sub>√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π].

A fixed α gives a nearly square output. For a sine, α is varied by cosine-wave crossing: a reference Vr sin ωot is compared with a cosine timing wave Vc cos ωt locked to the supply, and an SCR is fired where they cross, so cos α follows the reference:

blocks.where: r = V<sub>r</sub>/V<sub>c</sub> is the modulation ratio and ω<sub>o</sub> = 2πf<sub>o</sub>. With continuous current the local average output is (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos α = (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) r sin ω<sub>o</sub>t, so the largest fundamental a single-phase group can give has peak 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 0.9 V<sub>s</sub>, which is 146 V RMS from a 230 V supply.

blocks.text: The fewer supply pieces per output half cycle, the poorer the sine, so a common rule of thumb keeps f<sub>o</sub> ≤ f<sub>s</sub>/3, about 16.7 Hz from 50 Hz.

Step-up means f<sub>o</sub> > f<sub>s</sub>: the output must reverse several times inside one supply half cycle. When an SCR must stop, the supply has not reversed across it, so natural commutation cannot turn it off. Step-up cycloconverters need forced commutation or turn-off devices such as GTOs or IGBTs, and are rarely built because an inverter does the job more simply.

sections.h3: Circulating current, power factor and uses

blocks.text: In non-circulating mode, the outgoing group is blocked when the load current reaches zero and the incoming group fired after a short dead time. It needs current-zero sensing and distorts the output at each changeover, but needs no reactor.

In circulating-current mode, both groups are fired all the time with αP + αN = 180°, so their average voltages match. Their instantaneous voltages differ, so a current circulates between them, limited by an intergroup reactor. Changeover is smooth, at the cost of the size and loss of the reactor.

The input current lags as in any phase-controlled rectifier, with displacement factor close to cos α for an inductive load. Near an output zero α is near 90°, so the input power factor is poor at low output voltage. Uses: kilns, mills, mine hoists and ship propulsion, where motors run at a few hertz with very large torque.

examples.question: A single-phase bridge cycloconverter is fed from 230 V, 50 Hz and supplies a 10 Ω resistive load at one third of the supply frequency. Both groups are fired at α = 60° in every half cycle. Find the output frequency and period, the RMS output voltage and current, the load power and the input power factor.
steps: f<sub>o</sub> = 50/3 = 16.67 Hz, so T<sub>o</sub> = 1/16.67 = 60 ms: the P group gives three positive humps (30 ms), then the N group three negative humps.
Each hump is a half sine conducted from 60° to 180°, as in an AC voltage controller. α = π/3, sin 120° = 0.866: bracket = (π − π/3 + 0.433)/π = (2.094 + 0.433)/π = 0.8045.
P = 206.3²/10 = 4256 W. Input power factor = V<sub>o</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = 206.3/230 = 0.897.
examples.answer: f<sub>o</sub> = 16.67 Hz, T<sub>o</sub> = 60 ms, V<sub>o</sub> = 206.3 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 20.63 A, P = 4.26 kW, power factor 0.897.

examples.question: A single-phase bridge cycloconverter on 230 V, 50 Hz must give a 10 Hz output of 100 V RMS (fundamental) into a strongly inductive load, using cosine-wave crossing. Find the largest fundamental it can give, the modulation ratio r, and the firing angle of the P group at output angles ω<sub>o</sub>t = 0°, 30°, 60° and 90°.
steps: Check the frequency: 10 Hz ≤ 50/3 = 16.7 Hz, so the waveform quality is acceptable. Each output half cycle (50 ms) holds five supply half cycles.
V<sub>m</sub> = 230√2 = 325.3 V. The largest fundamental has peak 2V<sub>m</sub>/π = 2 × 325.3/π = 207.1 V, which is 146.4 V RMS.
Check at 90°: (2V<sub>m</sub>/π) cos 46.9° = 207.1 × 0.683 = 141.4 V, the wanted peak.
examples.answer: Largest fundamental 146.4 V RMS, r = 0.683, α = 90.0°, 70.0°, 53.7° and 46.9°; past 90° of the output the angles repeat in reverse, and the N group then does the same for the negative half cycle.

traps: Drawing a DC link or smoothing capacitor inside a cycloconverter. The two groups join the supply straight to the load.
Asking a single-phase group for more fundamental than 2V<sub>m</sub>/π peak. From 230 V that is 146 V RMS; a 200 V RMS output would need r = 1.37, above the limit of 1.
Writing that a step-down cycloconverter needs forced commutation. Step-down works with natural (line) commutation; step-up is the one that needs forced commutation or turn-off devices.
Releasing the incoming group in non-circulating mode before the load current is zero. Both groups then conduct together and short the supply.

quiz.q: How many SCRs does a single-phase bridge cycloconverter use, and how many does a three-phase to three-phase one use?
quiz.a: Eight for the single-phase bridge (two bridges of four). Three-phase to three-phase: 18 with three-pulse groups, 36 with six-pulse bridges.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a cycloconverter and an AC voltage controller?
quiz.a: A cycloconverter changes the output frequency; an AC voltage controller keeps the supply frequency and changes only the RMS voltage.

quiz.q: Why does a cycloconverter need two converter groups?
quiz.a: The load current must reverse every output half cycle, and a thyristor converter passes current one way only. The P group carries the positive current, the N group the negative current.

quiz.q: Why does a step-up cycloconverter need forced commutation?
quiz.a: Its output reverses several times inside one supply half cycle. When an SCR must stop conducting, the supply voltage across it has not reversed, so it cannot turn off naturally.

quiz.q: Repeat worked example 1 with α = 90°. Find V<sub>o</sub> and P.
In worked example 2, find α at ω<sub>o</sub>t = 45°.
Compare the circulating and non-circulating modes on waveform, size and efficiency.
quiz.a: Circulating: both groups always fired, smooth changeover and continuous current, but an intergroup reactor that adds size and loss. Non-circulating: no reactor and better efficiency, but a dead time at each current zero, which distorts the output and needs current-zero sensing.

quiz.q: Why is the input power factor of a cycloconverter poor when its output voltage is low?
quiz.a: Low output means cos α is small, so α is near 90° for most of each output cycle. The input current then lags the supply voltage by a large angle, as in a controlled rectifier at large α.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most new drives use back-to-back inverters or the matrix converter; cycloconverters remain in very large, slow drives such as gearless ore mills. Search for "gearless mill drive cycloconverter", "cosine wave crossing control" and "cycloconverter circulating current".
